Till
til
prep. and conj. of time (rendering Hebrew 'ad, Greek heos); distinguish the verb till, to cultivate
From Saxon til, to or unto, a preposition of limit. It marks the boundary of a duration — the point up to which something continues. The verb to till, meaning to cultivate the ground, is a wholly separate word, and the Authorized Version uses both.

Biblical Definition

Till marks the end of a duration: the point at which a state ceases. Its most solemn use fixes the entrance of sin into a creature made without it: “Thou wast perfect in thy ways from the day that thou wast created, till iniquity was found in thee” (Ezekiel 28:15). Everything before that word was good; everything after is ruin, and the single conjunction carries the whole fall. It also marks patient forbearance. The dresser of the vineyard pleads for the barren fig tree: “let it alone this year also, till I shall dig about it, and dung it” (Luke 13:8) — a reprieve with a limit and a labour attached to it. The Song uses it to forbid the forcing of love: “that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please” (Song of Solomon 2:7), thrice repeated in the book, a charge against haste in the one matter where haste is most tempting. And Christ uses it to govern the conduct of His messengers in a strange city: “there abide till ye go thence” (Matthew 10:11). The word to distinguish from all these is the verb of Genesis 3:23, “to till the ground”.

Webster 1828 Definition

A preposition and conjunction of time, marking the limit up to which something continues; until. Distinguish the verb to till, to cultivate. In Scripture it fixes the entrance of iniquity into a perfect creature and the term of God's forbearance.

expand to see more

TILL, prep. [Sax. til, to.] To the time of; until; as, wait till morning.

2. As a conjunction, to the time when; as, abide till I come.

3. TILL, v.t. [Sax. tilian, to labor.] To cultivate; to prepare and use for the production of crops. A wholly distinct word.

4. TILL, n. A money drawer in a shop or counter.

5. In Scripture, till iniquity was found in thee, Ezek. 28; till I shall dig about it, and dung it, Luke 13.

Key Scripture

Ezekiel 28:15 — "Thou wast perfect in thy ways from the day that thou wast created, till iniquity was found in thee."

Luke 13:8 — "And he answering said unto him, Lord, let it alone this year also, till I shall dig about it, and dung it:"

Song of Solomon 2:7 — "I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please."

Genesis 3:23 — "Therefore the LORD God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from whence he was taken."

Modern Corruption

God's forbearance is regularly mistaken for indifference or for permanence. Scripture's till keeps a term on it: the fig tree is spared this year also, the vinedresser digs and dungs, and then the matter is settled one way or the other.

expand to see more

The parable in Luke 13 is unusually exact about mercy. The tree has had three years and produced nothing; the owner's judgment is entirely just; and the dresser asks not for indefinite reprieve but for one more season with work done to it. Peter explains the same principle at the level of history: the Lord is not slack concerning His promise but is longsuffering, not willing that any should perish. Delay is mercy, not slackness, and it is not endless. To read God's patience as evidence that judgment will not come is the reasoning of the scoffers Peter describes.

Ezekiel 28:15 supplies the other half. The creature described was perfect in his ways from the day of his creation — a statement no one could have inferred, and one that forecloses any doctrine making evil eternal or making God its author. Iniquity was found in him; it had a beginning within a will that had been made good. This is the ground of the Confession's careful statement that God is not the author of sin, and that the creature's fall proceeded from himself. Between that till and the till of the fig tree stands the whole history of God's dealing with rebels.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'ad is the preposition of limit, up to and including; Greek uses heos with the same force. The verb till renders Hebrew 'abad, to serve or work the ground, an unrelated root.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'ad (H5704) — as far as, up to, until; the preposition of temporal and spatial limit.

Greek heos (G2193) — until, as far as; the ordinary conjunction of duration in the New Testament.

Hebrew 'avlah (H5766) — iniquity, unrighteousness; what was found in the creature of Ezekiel 28:15.

Hebrew 'abad (H5647) — to work, serve, till the ground; the root behind the unrelated verb to till.

Greek makrothumia (G3115) — longsuffering, patience; the disposition behind every scriptural reprieve.

Usage

"Of the moment sin entered a creature made perfect: till iniquity was found in thee (Ezekiel 28:15)."

"Of a reprieve granted with a term and a labour attached: let it alone this year also, till I shall dig about it (Luke 13:8)."

"Of love not to be forced or hurried: that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please (Song of Solomon 2:7)."
